newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FEATURE - Kazakh village tries to survive farm reforms.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Kazakh village tries to survive farm reforms.

text.p: "Labour is the source of all riches," proclaims a faded Soviet-era poster in this destitute village at the heart of Kazakhstan's grain belt.

For desperate villagers, who work hard but have not been paid for years, those words are just another bitter reminder of past ideological certainties, present financial woes and future fears for a neglected sector of the Kazakh economy.
"People have not been getting money for more than three years," said Natalia, a village accountant. "Farmers get coupons they swap for bread and sometimes for meat or hay."
Salaries -- calculated but never paid in the national tenge currency -- average around $30 a month.
"We are poor, and the village has no money in its bank account," Natalia said.
"This is not life but an attempt to survive," said Maria, Natalia's friend. "Things are going from bad to worse, and there is no ray of hope."
A spirit of neglect is omnipresent.
Agricultural machinery looks abandoned, rusting in the knee-high grass, while crumbling cattle-sheds with broken windows and holed roofs stand empty.
Three years ago, Yelizavetinka farm kept more than 1,000 cows in addition to growing grain, but only about 100 have survived culls necessitated by lack of fodder.

Yet the drudgery in Yelizavetinka -- with a population of 3,800 people and located 1,300 km (800 miles) from the capital Almaty, in the centre of Kazakhstan's largest northern grain belt -- is little different in other villages, locals say.
AGRICULTURAL REFORM JUST MEANT CHANGING NAMES
Yelizavetinka's impoverished residents say their hardship stems from a failed attempt to reform agriculture.

Kazakhstan's agricultural sector still produces 20 percent of the Central Asian state's gross domestic product, according to official statistics. It inherited from the Soviet Union large state-run farms specialising mostly in grain and cattle.

But the Soviet Union's overnight collapse in late 1991 meant the cash-hungry government of independent Kazakhstan chased foreign investment for decaying but potentially lucrative communications, oil and gas and metals industries.
It patently overlooked the needs of agriculture.
Delayed reforms and scarce financing have led to the collapse of Kazakhstan's agriculture, which is officially said to be no longer in state hands.
But for Yelizavetinka -- a sovkhoz, or "state farm", in Soviet days -- agricultural reform and a new property status amounted to little more than a change in name.

Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev, who enjoys sweeping executive powers in a vast steppeland country five times the size of France yet populated by just 16.7 million people, demanded earlier this year that reforms be accelerated.
In April, Yelizavetinka, like many other Kazakh villages, was officially informed it was no longer a sovkhoz but a "TOO" -- an "Association with Limited Responsibility".
"We are now officially private owners but nothing has changed -- we are getting even poorer," Natalia said.
Higher taxes imposed on the village after changing Yelizavetinka's status seem to be the only "gain" so far.
Rumours that the authorities might now impose taxes on the cattle the farmers keep at their homesteads has clearly alarmed the "private" village's population.
"We have nothing. Everything -- machinery and other costly equipment -- was stolen long ago in this general chaos and uncertainty," said another villager who declined to be named.
COLLAPSE OF AGRICULTURE HITS GRAIN GROWING
Yelizavetinka still produces grain, but a lack of machinery and fertilisers means yields are meagre.

"We have no money, and every year we barter grain from the future harvest for fuel when sowing starts. But when the harvest is over, we sometimes do not have enough grain to pay our creditors," Natalia said.
The village lies in the Akmola region, Kazakhstan's main producer of grain, and Yelizavetinka's grain-growing record these days appears typical of the whole region.

"The general culture of farming has fallen dramatically," said Onal Shegebayev, director of the Grain Farming Research Institute located 30 km (20 miles) from Yelizavetinka. "Weeds alone consume up to 40 percent of grain harvest each year."
He said last year's harvesting in the region dragged on for 70 days compared with a tempo of 30 to 45 days in Soviet days.
"Unfortunately, attempts to reform agriculture have not improved people's responsibility for the results of their labour," he added.

Shegebayev said that this year Kazakhstan -- still among major grain producers in the former Soviet Union -- might harvest 14 million tonnes of grain, but added that this amount would be just a half of what it produced in Soviet times.

Yet whatever its present-day hardships, Yelizavetinka, surprisingly, seems to be backing Nazarbayev, who has repeatedly said inter-ethnic accord among Kazakhstan's 100-plus nationalities and general political stability are a result of his policies.

"In our village there are people of different nationalities, but we live in harmony," said Maria, an ethnic Bulgarian resettled to Kazakhstan from Moldova in 1968. "And -- thanks to the government -- there are no wars as in other republics of the former Soviet Union."
